tags.description: How a kimono is put on.

posts.title: What to wear under a kimono
posts.excerpt: Less than you think. A thin top, leggings in winter, and the rest we lend. Sayo on the layers that make a kimono sit well.
posts.content:
Most guests arrive worried that they have brought the wrong clothes. There are no wrong clothes: everything that touches the kimono is ours, washed after every wear.

The layers

Next to the skin goes the hadajuban, a thin cotton slip. Over it the nagajuban, the under-kimono whose collar shows at your neck. A little padding at the waist evens the line so the obi sits flat.

What to bring

A thin vest and leggings in winter, nothing extra in summer. Wear your hair loose or tied low, and we will set it.

posts.title: Six ways to tie an obi
posts.excerpt: From the plain drum knot to the butterfly. Which knot suits which kimono, and which one lasts best through a long day of walking.
posts.content:
The obi is where a kimono gets its character. We offer six knots, and each says something different.

The drum

Otaiko, the drum knot, is the quiet square most women in Kyoto wear. It is flat against the back and lasts a whole day.

The butterfly

For yukata and furisode, a bow tied high and wide. It is cheerful and best for evenings.

posts.title: A morning walk from Kiyomizu to Gion
posts.excerpt: Leave before the buses arrive. Our favourite route down the old stone lanes, with two tea stops and a quiet temple garden.
posts.content:
The lanes below Kiyomizu are at their best before nine. Dress early, step out of the house and turn downhill.

Sannen-zaka and Ninen-zaka

Take the stone steps slowly in zori. The wooden fronts are still shuttered and the light is soft.

To Gion

Through the Yasaka shrine gate, along Hanamikoji, and home for tea by eleven.

posts.title: Yukata evenings on the river
posts.excerpt: In July and August the rack turns to cotton. How a yukata differs from a kimono, and why the evening is the time to wear one.
posts.content:
A yukata is unlined cotton, worn without an under-kimono. It is light, simple and quick to dress.

When to wear one

Summer festivals, fireworks and evenings by the Kamo river. In the heat of the afternoon a parasol helps more than anything.

posts.title: The small things that finish a kimono
posts.excerpt: A hair ornament, a bag, the right zori. Mei on choosing accessories that sit quietly with the colour of the silk.
posts.content:
A kimono is finished by small things. Choose one that echoes a colour in the silk and leave the rest plain.

The ornament

A single kanzashi, silk flower or silver, set low at the back of the hair.

posts.title: Caring for old silk
posts.excerpt: Why we air every kimono on a bamboo pole after each wear, and the three things that keep silk soft for decades.
posts.content:
Silk wants air, dark and patience. After each wear we hang every kimono upstairs for a night before it is pressed.

Folding

A kimono folds along its own seams into a flat rectangle. Folded right, it never needs ironing.
